content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

I'm acting as your Facilitator. Before we talk about any screens or features, I'd like to understand the goal behind this, so we build the right thing.

A bookmark app can mean very different things depending on what's actually bothering you today. So let me start with the "why":

**When this bookmark app is finished and working well, what would be different from how you handle things now?**

For example — are you trying to solve something like:
- "I save links but can never find them again later"
- "My bookmarks are scattered across different browsers/devices and I want them in one place"
- "I collect links to read later but they pile up and I lose track"
- "I want to organize links for a specific purpose (research, shopping, work projects)"
- something else entirely?

You don't need to pick from that list — it's just to give you a sense of the kind of answer I'm after. Tell me in your own words what's frustrating you now, and what you're hoping this changes.

Honestly, it's a mix of a few of those, but if I had to name the thing that bugs me most: I save links all the time and then they just... vanish into a pile. I can never find the one I want later, and half of them are things I meant to read and never got back to.

So really what I want is a single place where I dump every interesting link, and then actually be able to *find it again* — search it, or narrow down to a topic, without scrolling forever. And I'd love a way to tell apart "stuff I still need to read" from "stuff I've already dealt with," because right now everything blurs together.

The other quiet frustration is that when I paste a link, all I get is a raw web address with no clue what it was. I'd want it to actually show me what the page is — its name, maybe a little description — so I'm not staring at a wall of gibberish URLs.

Does that give you enough to start, or do you want me to go deeper on any of it?

That's a really clear picture — thank you. Let me play back what I heard to make sure I've got the direction right.

The heart of it isn't "saving" links — that part already works fine for you. The pain is everything *after* saving. So the real goal is:

> **"A single place where I can dump any interesting link and reliably get it back later — instead of watching it disappear into a pile I can't search."**

And underneath that, three things have to be true for it to actually feel solved:

1. **Findability** — I can search or narrow down to a topic and land on the link I want, without endless scrolling.
2. **Status** — I can tell "still need to read" apart from "already dealt with," so the unread stuff doesn't blur into everything else.
3. **Recognizability** — a saved link shows me what the page actually *is* (its name, maybe a short description), not a raw URL.

One scope question, because it changes what we build toward:

**When you imagine "finally solved" — is the win mostly that you can find any old link on demand (a reliable personal library / archive)? Or is the bigger win that the "meant to read" pile actually gets smaller because the app helps you get back to it (more of a read-it-later workflow)?**

Both are valid — but one of them is the thing you'd be quietly measuring success by, and I want to aim at that one. Which rings truer?

Your playback is spot on — those three are exactly it.

But I'll be honest, I don't love being made to pick one, because if I'm quietly measuring success, it's really the first one: I want a reliable personal library where I can find any old link on demand. That's the foundation. If that's not there, nothing else matters.

That said, the "meant to read" pile isn't a throwaway — it's a real, everyday thing for me. I don't need the app to nag me or build some elaborate workflow, but I do need to be able to flip to just my unread stuff and work through it, then mark things off as I go. Think of it less as a separate mode and more as one view sitting on top of the same library.

So: library first, with the read-later pile as a lens I can switch into whenever I want. Does treating it that way cause you a problem, or can we aim at both with the library as the anchor?

## How I'd build it

**The shape: it's *yours*, on *your* machine.**
Everything you approved points the same direction — private, no accounts, works when you're offline, exportable, never held hostage. So the app keeps your library **on your own computer**, not on some company's server. Your links, notes, labels, read-later pile, and every saved copy live locally. That's what makes "private, just me" and "never trapped" true at the foundation rather than as a promise.

**The one real decision I need you on.**
There's a security rule in browsers that matters here: a plain web page you open *isn't allowed* to reach out and read other websites. That's normally good — but two of your features depend on exactly that: **fetching a link's name/description**, and **keeping a saved copy** of a page. A bare web page simply can't do those on its own. So we pick one of two ways to give it that reach:

- **Option A — a browser add-on (extension).** It installs into your browser and can see the page you're *actually looking at* — which makes capturing the name and a faithful saved copy clean and reliable, gives you a "save this page" button right where you read, needs **nothing running in the background**, and lives right in your browser where you already are. Your library opens as a full tab. Cost: you install it once per browser.
- **Option B — a small companion program** that runs quietly on your computer and does the fetching/snapshotting, with the library as an ordinary web page. Cost: it's a background program you have to have running.

**My recommendation is A, the add-on** — it fits everything you told me best: capture and saved copies work well, it's private, there's nothing to babysit, and it's *in the browser where you live*. B is the fallback if you'd rather not install an extension.
